Smale’s mean value constant and admissible univalent Blaschke pairs

Aneesh Jatar    Tuen-Wai Ng
Abstract

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the class of polynomials PP of degree at least 22 with P⁡(0)=0P(0)=0, P′​(0)=1P^{\prime}(0)=1, let S⁡(P)=minP′​(c)=0⁡|P⁡(c)/c|S(P)=\min_{P^{\prime}(c)=0}|P(c)/c| and let ℳ=supP∈𝒫S⁡(P)\mathcal{M}=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}S(P) be Smale’s mean value constant. Smale proved that ℳ≤4\mathcal{M}\leq 4, observed that ℳ≥1\mathcal{M}\geq 1, and asked whether ℳ=1\mathcal{M}=1. We show that ℳ\mathcal{M} coincides with

ℬ=sup1B⁡(0),\mathcal{B}=\sup\frac{1}{B(0)},

the supremum running over pairs (W,B)(W,B) in which WW is a normalised univalent map of the standard unit disk 𝔻\mathbb{D} and BB is a finite Blaschke product with B⁡(0)>0B(0)>0 such that W​BWB is locally univalent in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. Smale’s question is therefore a problem in univalent function theory. We also introduce the degree-restricted constants ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} for BB with deg⁡B≤d\deg B\leq d and show that

1.1018586788​…=80816656≤ℬ1<75=1.1832159566​…1.1018586788\ldots=\sqrt{\frac{8081}{6656}}\leq\mathcal{B}_{1}<\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}}=1.1832159566\ldots

This implies that ℳ>1.1018\mathcal{M}>1.1018 and we also show that there are polynomials of arbitrarily large degree with S⁡(P)>1.1018S(P)>1.1018. The polynomial construction behind these results also settles Problems 1A and 1B of Smale’s 1981 paper. For P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} and an integer k≥2k\geq 2 let Sk​(P)=minP′​(c)=0⁡|P(k)​(0)/k!|1/(k−1)​|P⁡(c)|S_{k}(P)=\min_{P^{\prime}(c)=0}|P^{(k)}(0)/k!|^{1/(k-1)}|P(c)|. Smale proved, by Löwner’s coefficient estimate for inverses of univalent functions, that supP∈𝒫Sk​(P)≤Ck1/(k−1)<4\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}S_{k}(P)\leq C_{k}^{1/(k-1)}<4, where CkC_{k} is the kk-th Catalan number and he asked whether the constant 44 (Problem 1A), or the constant 2=C22=C_{2} for k=2k=2 (Problem 1B), can be reduced. We prove that supP∈𝒫Sk​(P)=Ck1/(k−1)\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}S_{k}(P)=C_{k}^{1/(k-1)} for every k≥2k\geq 2. Hence the constants 44 and 22 cannot be reduced and the answers to both problems are negative.

1 Setting and results

1.1 Smale’s constant

As a byproduct of Smale’s study of the complexity of Newton’s method [25], he introduced and studied the following constants.

Let 𝒫d\mathcal{P}_{d} be the class of polynomials PP of degree d≥2d\geq 2 with P⁡(0)=0P(0)=0, P′​(0)=1P^{\prime}(0)=1, and 𝒫=⋃d≥2𝒫d\mathcal{P}=\bigcup_{d\geq 2}\mathcal{P}_{d}. For P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} put q⁡(w)=P⁡(w)/wq(w)=P(w)/w, a polynomial with q⁡(0)=1q(0)=1 and deg⁡q=deg⁡P−1≥1\deg q=\deg P-1\geq 1. Smale’s quantity is

S⁡(P):=minP′​(c)=0⁡|P⁡(c)c|=minP′​(c)=0⁡|q⁡(c)|,ℳd:=supP∈𝒫dS⁡(P),ℳ:=supP∈𝒫S⁡(P).S(P):=\min_{P^{\prime}(c)=0}\Bigl|\frac{P(c)}{c}\Bigr|=\min_{P^{\prime}(c)=0}|q(c)|,\qquad\mathcal{M}_{d}:=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}}S(P),\qquad\mathcal{M}:=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}S(P).

(The origin is not a critical point, since P′​(0)=1P^{\prime}(0)=1.) The quantity S⁡(P)S(P) is invariant under P⁡(w)↦λ−1​P​(λ​w)P(w)\mapsto\lambda^{-1}P(\lambda w). Smale [25] proved S⁡(P)≤4S(P)\leq 4 for all P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P}, i.e. ℳ≤4\mathcal{M}\leq 4. He also noticed that P⁡(w)=w−wd/dP(w)=w-w^{d}/d gives S⁡(P)=(d−1)/dS(P)=(d-1)/d, and asked whether ℳ=1\mathcal{M}=1 or even ℳd=(d−1)/d\mathcal{M}_{d}=(d-1)/d. This is Smale’s mean value conjecture, one of the three minor problems in his problem list for the next century [26]. The conjecture is true for d≤4d\leq 4 and for special classes of polynomials; the degree-dependent refinements ℳd≤4(d−2)/(d−1)\mathcal{M}_{d}\leq 4^{(d-2)/(d-1)} [2] and ℳd≤4−c/d\mathcal{M}_{d}\leq 4-c/\sqrt{d} [6] tend to 44 as d→∞d\to\infty. So ℳ≤4\mathcal{M}\leq 4 is still the best known upper bound for ℳ\mathcal{M} itself. See [6, 18, 14, 11] for surveys of the literature and the latest results.

In [1] a pre-release version of GPT-6 Astra produced a machine-checked (Lean 4/Mathlib) proof that the constant-11 form of the conjecture is false: there is a polynomial PP of large, unspecified degree with S⁡(P)>1S(P)>1. In [1], the counterexample is built in four steps: i) a locally univalent function of the form (z−z0)​Br​(W⁡(z))/Br​(W⁡(z0))(z-z_{0})B_{r}(W(z))/B_{r}(W(z_{0})) is constructed on the quartic lemniscate K={|z4+64i|≤4097}K=\{|z^{4}+64i|\leq\sqrt{4097}\}, where W:K→𝔻¯W:K\to\overline{\mathbb{D}} is a conformal map and BrB_{r} is a Blaschke factor; ii) it is approximated by a polynomial f0f_{0}; and iii) the primitive of a high even power of the quartic q⁡(z)=z4+64​iq(z)=z^{4}+64i is added to f0f_{0}, which forces all critical points of the polynomial Pn=f0+∫q2​nP_{n}=f_{0}+\int q^{2n} into a thin collar around ∂K\partial K; iv) rescale PnP_{n} to get a polynomial P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} so that S⁡(P)>1S(P)>1. The same argument can be further developed to give for example S⁡(P)>1+2−35S(P)>1+2^{-35}, but it is hard to push this approach to reach a lower bound like 1.10181.1018.

Motivated and based upon the GPT-6 Astra construction, in the present paper, we give two reformulations of Smale’s mean value problem by introducing two new constants 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} which arise (respectively) from two (equivalent) extremal problems for pairs of the form (f,Ω)(f,\Omega) and (W,B)(W,B), where f⁡(0)=0,f′​(0)=1f(0)=0,f^{\prime}(0)=1 is locally univalent in a neighbourhood of Ω¯\overline{\Omega} and Ω\Omega is a bounded, analytic Jordan domain containing the origin, while WW is a univalent function on the unit disk fixing the origin, and BB is a finite Blaschke product for which W​BWB is locally univalent on the unit disk. We show that 𝒜=ℳ=ℬ\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{B}. The definitions of 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} will be given in Section 4.1 and Section 1.2 respectively.

Smale’s paper [25] also contains a second family of extremal problems for critical values, which arises from the Taylor expansion of PP at the current point of the Newton iteration. For P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} and an integer k≥2k\geq 2 let

Sk​(P):=minP′​(c)=0⁡|P(k)​(0)k!|1k−1​|P⁡(c)|,𝒦d,k:=supP∈𝒫dSk​(P),𝒦k:=supP∈𝒫Sk​(P),𝒦:=supk≥2𝒦kS_{k}(P):=\min_{P^{\prime}(c)=0}\Bigl|\frac{P^{(k)}(0)}{k!}\Bigr|^{\frac{1}{k-1}}|P(c)|,\qquad\mathcal{K}_{d,k}:=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}}S_{k}(P),\qquad\mathcal{K}_{k}:=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}S_{k}(P),\qquad\mathcal{K}:=\sup_{k\geq 2}\mathcal{K}_{k}

(see Section 5 for the equivalent unnormalized form). Using Löwner’s theorem on the coefficients of inverses of univalent functions, Smale proved that 𝒦k≤Ck1/(k−1)<4\mathcal{K}_{k}\leq C_{k}^{1/(k-1)}<4, where Ck=(2​k)!k!​(k+1)!C_{k}=\frac{(2k)!}{k!\,(k+1)!} is the kk-th Catalan number, i.e. the modulus of the kk-th Taylor coefficient of the inverse Koebe function; hence 𝒦≤4\mathcal{K}\leq 4. He observed that 𝒦≥1\mathcal{K}\geq 1 and asked in Problem 1A of [25] whether the constant 44 can be reduced, possibly to 11, and in Problem 1B whether the constant 2=C22=C_{2} for k=2k=2 can be reduced to d−12​d\frac{d-1}{2d} for polynomials of degree dd. For the top coefficient k=dk=d, Dubinin [8] proved the sharp result 𝒦d,d=(d−1)d−d/(d−1)\mathcal{K}_{d,d}=(d-1)d^{-d/(d-1)}, so that Smale’s example w−wd/dw-w^{d}/d is extremal for k=dk=d, while the lower bound of d−12​d\frac{d-1}{2d} for Kd,2K_{d,2} is known to be false for infinitely many degrees dd (see the thesis of Choi [4] and also Cheung [3]). On the other hand, despite the bound of d−12​d\frac{d-1}{2d} being false for infinitely many degrees, it is not known whether the constant 22 can be reduced at all. We will refer to this more general question again as “Problem 1B” in the remainder of this paper. We observe that the Runge–Hilbert construction which gives 𝒜≤ℳ\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{M} (Proposition 4.3) works equally well for the quantities SkS_{k} and, when applied to the inverse Koebe function, produces the reverse inequality 𝒦k≥Ck1/(k−1)\mathcal{K}_{k}\geq C_{k}^{1/(k-1)}. Thus 𝒦k=Ck1/(k−1)\mathcal{K}_{k}=C_{k}^{1/(k-1)} for every k≥2k\geq 2, 𝒦2=2\mathcal{K}_{2}=2 and 𝒦=4\mathcal{K}=4. In conclusion, Smale’s constants 44 and 22 cannot be reduced, and Problems 1A and 1B are answered in the negative.

1.2 Admissible univalent Blaschke pairs

Write 𝔻={z∈ℂ:|z|<1}\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}, 𝕋=∂𝔻\mathbb{T}=\partial\mathbb{D}, D⁡(w,ρ)={ζ:|ζ−w|<ρ}D(w,\rho)=\{\zeta:|\zeta-w|<\rho\}, and let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the class of functions WW holomorphic and univalent in 𝔻\mathbb{D} with W⁡(0)=0W(0)=0 and W′​(0)=1W^{\prime}(0)=1.

A finite Blaschke product is a function

B⁡(z)=λ​∏k=1nz−ak1−ak¯​z,|λ|=1,ak∈𝔻,n≥0,B(z)=\lambda\prod_{k=1}^{n}\frac{z-a_{k}}{1-\overline{a_{k}}z},\qquad|\lambda|=1,\quad a_{k}\in\mathbb{D},\quad n\geq 0,

zeros being repeated according to multiplicity and n=deg⁡Bn=\deg B. We shall use the following standard facts: BB is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}} (its poles 1/ak¯1/\overline{a_{k}} lie outside 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}), |B|=1|B|=1 on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, and |B|<1|B|<1 in 𝔻\mathbb{D} if n≥1n\geq 1. If no aka_{k} is 00, the normalization B⁡(0)>0B(0)>0 fixes the unimodular constant, namely λ=∏k(−ak¯/|ak|)\lambda=\prod_{k}(-\overline{a_{k}}/|a_{k}|), and then

B⁡(0)=∏k=1n|ak|.B(0)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}|a_{k}|. (1)

A pair consisting of a univalent function WW and a finite Blaschke product BB is called a univalent Blaschke pair or simply a pair (W,B)(W,B). To reformulate Smale’s mean value constant ℳ\mathcal{M}, we also introduce the following

Definition 1.1.

A pair (W,B)(W,B) is (normalized) admissible if

  1. 1.

    W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S};

  2. 2.

    BB is a finite Blaschke product with B⁡(0)>0B(0)>0;

  3. 3.

    F:=W​BF:=WB satisfies F′​(z)≠0F^{\prime}(z)\neq 0 for all z∈𝔻z\in\mathbb{D}.

The constant B≡1B\equiv 1 is allowed. We set

ℬ:=sup{1B⁡(0):(W,B)admissible},ℬd:=sup{1B⁡(0):(W,B)admissible,degB≤d}.\mathcal{B}:=\sup\Bigl\{\frac{1}{B(0)}:(W,B)\ \text{admissible}\Bigr\},\qquad\mathcal{B}_{d}:=\sup\Bigl\{\frac{1}{B(0)}:(W,B)\ \text{admissible},\ \deg B\leq d\Bigr\}.

An admissible pair is regular if WW extends to a univalent function on a neighbourhood of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}} and F′≠0F^{\prime}\neq 0 on 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}.

Since (W,1)(W,1) is admissible for every W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S}, ℬ≥ℬd≥1\mathcal{B}\geq\mathcal{B}_{d}\geq 1. Note that B⁡(0)≠0B(0)\neq 0 is forced by condition 3 because a zero of BB at the origin would make FF vanish to order ≥2\geq 2 there, so F′​(0)=0F^{\prime}(0)=0. For the same reason all zeros of BB are simple. Observe also that F′​(0)=W′​(0)​B​(0)=B⁡(0)F^{\prime}(0)=W^{\prime}(0)B(0)=B(0). The normalizations W′​(0)=1W^{\prime}(0)=1 and B⁡(0)>0B(0)>0 are harmless: for any univalent WW with W⁡(0)=0W(0)=0 and any finite Blaschke product BB with (W​B)′≠0(WB)^{\prime}\neq 0 on 𝔻\mathbb{D}, the pair (W/W′​(0),B​|B⁡(0)|/B⁡(0))(W/W^{\prime}(0),\,B\,|B(0)|/B(0)) is admissible with the same value 1/|B⁡(0)|1/|B(0)|. We will thus refer to any pair (W,B)(W,B) with W⁡(0)=0W(0)=0 univalent on 𝔻\mathbb{D}, BB a finite Blaschke product, such that W​BWB is locally univalent on 𝔻\mathbb{D} as admissible in the sequel.

Throughout we use the notation

F=W​B,g=z​W′W,Φ=z​F′F=g+z​B′B.F=WB,\qquad g=\frac{zW^{\prime}}{W},\qquad\Phi=\frac{zF^{\prime}}{F}=g+\frac{zB^{\prime}}{B}.

Since W⁡(z)=z+O⁡(z2)W(z)=z+O(z^{2}) and W≠0W\neq 0 on 𝔻∖{0}\mathbb{D}\setminus\{0\}, the function gg is holomorphic on 𝔻\mathbb{D} with g⁡(0)=1g(0)=1; Φ\Phi is meromorphic on 𝔻\mathbb{D}, Φ⁡(0)=1\Phi(0)=1, and its poles in 𝔻\mathbb{D} are exactly the distinct zeros of BB (all simple). Moreover, Φ\Phi has no zeros in 𝔻\mathbb{D}.

1.3 Main results

Theorem 1.2.

ℳ=ℬ.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}\ =\ \mathcal{B}.

The inequality ℳ≤ℬ\mathcal{M}\leq\mathcal{B} is proved in Section 3 by a Riemann map of a sublevel component of P⁡(w)/wP(w)/w. The inequality ℬ≤ℳ\mathcal{B}\leq\mathcal{M} is then proved in Section 4, through the intermediate constant 𝒜\mathcal{A} of Section 4.1: we show ℬ≤𝒜≤ℳ\mathcal{B}\leq\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{M}, so that in fact ℳ=ℬ=𝒜\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{A} (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 1.3.

For every admissible pair (W,B)(W,B) one has B⁡(0)≥m⁡(W)≥14B(0)\geq m(W)\geq\tfrac{1}{4}, where m⁡(W)=dist⁡(0,∂W⁡(𝔻))m(W)=\dist(0,\partial W(\mathbb{D})). Hence ℬ≤4\mathcal{B}\leq 4, and by Theorem 1.2 this recovers Smale’s theorem ℳ≤4\mathcal{M}\leq 4. Moreover, for every d≥1d\geq 1,

ℬd<4−529576​(log⁡2)2d2,\mathcal{B}_{d}<4-\frac{529}{576}\frac{(\log 2)^{2}}{d^{2}},

and

1.1018586788​…=80816656≤ℬ1<75=1.1832159566​…1.1018586788\ldots=\sqrt{\frac{8081}{6656}}\leq\mathcal{B}_{1}<\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}}=1.1832159566\ldots

Hence ℳ>1.1018\mathcal{M}>1.1018, which improves the result ℳ>1\mathcal{M}>1 in [1], and ℳd>1.1018\mathcal{M}_{d}>1.1018 for all large dd.

Theorem 1.4.

For every integer k≥2k\geq 2,

𝒦k=supP∈𝒫Sk​(P)=Ck1k−1,Ck=(2​k)!k!​(k+1)!,\mathcal{K}_{k}=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}S_{k}(P)=C_{k}^{\frac{1}{k-1}},\qquad C_{k}=\frac{(2k)!}{k!\,(k+1)!},

and for every A<Ck1/(k−1)A<C_{k}^{1/(k-1)} there are polynomials P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} of arbitrarily large degree with Sk​(P)>AS_{k}(P)>A. Consequently 𝒦2=2\mathcal{K}_{2}=2 and 𝒦=4\mathcal{K}=4; in particular Smale’s Problems 1A and 1B in [25] have negative answers. Moreover for Problem 1B, Kd,2K_{d,2} can be made arbitrarily close to 22 for sufficiently large degrees dd.

The identification ℳ=ℬ\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{B} recasts Smale’s mean value problem entirely within univalent function theory and yields the improved quantitative lower bound ℳ>1.1018\mathcal{M}>1.1018 and hence a new disproof of Smale’s mean value conjecture. This identification also makes available the full toolkit of univalent function theory (e.g., Grunsky inequalities) for studying the new questions of determining the exact values of the constants ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} and whether ℬ=4\mathcal{B}=4. The same approach also suggests a systematic route for translating other classical extremal problems involving polynomials into questions about pairs of univalent maps and Blaschke products. In fact, Sheil-Small has already suggested this translation in [24, Chapter 10] and our reformulation is linked to a special case of Sheil-Small’s translation. Theorem 1.4 is an instance of this route in the opposite direction: the extremal function of univalent function theory (the Koebe function) is converted into extremal polynomials for Smale’s constants 𝒦k\mathcal{K}_{k}.

The paper recalls Smale’s constant ℳ\mathcal{M} and introduces the reformulation ℬ\mathcal{B} via admissible univalent Blaschke pairs in Section 1.1–1.2. Section 2 contains an auxiliary regularization result (not needed for the main theorem). The inequality ℳ≤ℬ\mathcal{M}\leq\mathcal{B} is established in Section 3 by a Riemann-map construction from polynomials. In Section 4 the companion constant 𝒜\mathcal{A} is defined, the elementary inequality ℬ≤𝒜\mathcal{B}\leq\mathcal{A} is proved, and the only analytic step of the paper, 𝒜≤ℳ\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{M}, is obtained from Runge approximation and Hilbert’s Lemniscate Theorem; this gives ℳ=ℬ=𝒜\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{A} and the existence of infinitely many degrees dd with ℳd>1.1018\mathcal{M}_{d}>1.1018. Section 5 recalls Smale’s constants 𝒦d,k\mathcal{K}_{d,k}, 𝒦k\mathcal{K}_{k}, 𝒦\mathcal{K} and his Problems 1A and 1B, and combines a variant of Proposition 4.3 with Löwner’s theorem to prove Theorem 1.4. The degree-one lower bound appears in Section 6 via an explicit quartic and Dieudonné’s criterion, while the upper bounds ℬ≤4\mathcal{B}\leq 4, ℬd≤4−O⁡(1/d2)\mathcal{B}_{d}\leq 4-O(1/d^{2}) and ℬ1≤7/5\mathcal{B}_{1}\leq\sqrt{7/5} are obtained in Section 7 from the Koebe theorem, the Schwarz lemma, Pick’s omitted-value estimate and Grunsky’s inequality. Section 8 proves existence of admissible pairs of every degree, a necessary and (essentially) sufficient condition on WW for the existence of a nonconstant factor BB, attainment of each ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d}, and the strict inequalities of Theorem 1.3. Concluding remarks, open problems and dual constants are given in Section 9.

1.4 Standard tools

We collect the classical results used below, with references.

  • (T1)

    Koebe’s one-quarter theorem [9, Chapter 2]. For W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S}, W⁡(𝔻)⊃D⁡(0,1/4)W(\mathbb{D})\supset D(0,1/4).

  • (T2)

    Analytic boundaries [20, Chapter 3]. If Ω\Omega is a Jordan domain bounded by a real-analytic Jordan curve, the Riemann map 𝔻→Ω\mathbb{D}\to\Omega extends to a conformal (univalent holomorphic) map of a neighbourhood of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}; in particular it is Lipschitz on 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}} and maps 𝕋\mathbb{T} onto ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

  • (T3)

    Runge’s theorem [23, Ch. 13]. If K⊂ℂK\subset\mathbb{C} is compact with connected complement and pp is holomorphic on an open set containing KK, there are polynomials converging to pp uniformly on KK. By the Cauchy estimates the derivatives then converge uniformly on compact subsets of the interior of KK.

  • (T4)

    Proper self-maps of the disk [22, p.211-213]. If B:𝔻→𝔻B:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D} is holomorphic and proper, then BB is a finite Blaschke product.

  • (T5)

    Hilbert’s Lemniscate Theorem [13, 19]. Let UU be a closed topological annulus in ℂ\mathbb{C}. There is a nonconstant polynomial qq such that the entire lemniscate

    Γ={w∈ℂ:|q⁡(w)|=1}\Gamma=\{w\in\mathbb{C}:|q(w)|=1\}

    is an analytic Jordan curve contained in UU and separating its two boundary components. Applying the theorem to a smaller annulus, one may require Γ⊂int⁡U\Gamma\subset\Int U.

  • (T6)

    Riemann–Hurwitz count for a Jordan domain. Let CC be a Jordan domain bounded by an analytic Jordan curve γ\gamma, and let hh be holomorphic on a neighbourhood of C¯\overline{C} with |h|=1|h|=1 on γ\gamma, |h|<1|h|<1 in CC and h′≠0h^{\prime}\neq 0 on γ\gamma. If hh has mm zeros in CC (with multiplicity), then h′h^{\prime} has exactly m−1m-1 zeros in CC.

    Proof. h|γ:γ→𝕋h|_{\gamma}:\gamma\to\mathbb{T} is a local homeomorphism, hence a covering of some degree m′m^{\prime}, orientation preserving because |h|<1|h|<1 on the left of γ\gamma. By applying the argument principle to hh, m′=mm^{\prime}=m. If γ⁡(s)\gamma(s) is a positive parametrization, arg⁡dd​s​h​(γ⁡(s))=arg⁡h′​(γ⁡(s))+arg⁡γ′​(s)\arg\frac{d}{ds}h(\gamma(s))=\arg h^{\prime}(\gamma(s))+\arg\gamma^{\prime}(s) increases by 2​π​m2\pi m along γ\gamma, while arg⁡γ′\arg\gamma^{\prime} increases by 2​π2\pi (Hopf Umlaufsatz). Hence Δγ​arg⁡h′=2​π​(m−1)\Delta_{\gamma}\arg h^{\prime}=2\pi(m-1), and the argument principle applied to h′h^{\prime} gives the claim. ∎

4.1 𝒜=ℳ\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}

Proposition 4.3 suggests one may consider another reformulation of Smale’s mean value constant ℳ\mathcal{M} which we detail in this section.

In this section, a pair (f,Ω)(f,\Omega) will be called admissible if Ω\Omega is a bounded analytic Jordan domain containing the origin in its interior, and ff is a holomorphic function, locally univalent on a neighbourhood of Ω¯\overline{\Omega}, fixing the origin, with unit derivative at the origin. Set

𝒜:=sup{infz∈∂Ω|f⁡(z)z|:(f,Ω)​ is admissible}.\mathcal{A}:=\sup\{\inf_{z\in\partial\Omega}|\frac{f(z)}{z}|:(f,\Omega)\text{ is admissible}\}.

Since the pair (z,𝔻)(z,\mathbb{D}) is clearly admissible, 𝒜≥1\mathcal{A}\geq 1. Proposition 4.3 is exactly the statement that for each admissible pair (f,Ω)(f,\Omega) and each 0<A<infz∈∂Ω|f⁡(z)/z|0<A<\inf_{z\in\partial\Omega}|f(z)/z|, there is a corresponding polynomial P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} with S⁡(P)>AS(P)>A and hence

ℳ≥infz∈∂Ω|f⁡(z)z|.\mathcal{M}\ \geq\ \inf_{z\in\partial\Omega}\Bigl|\frac{f(z)}{z}\Bigr|.

This motivates the next theorem.

Theorem 4.4.
𝒜=ℳ\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}
Proof.

Proposition 4.3 immediately implies that 𝒜≤ℳ\mathcal{A}\leq\mathcal{M}. To prove 𝒜≥ℳ\mathcal{A}\geq\mathcal{M} we may assume without loss of generality that ℳ>1\mathcal{M}>1, for if ℳ≤1\mathcal{M}\leq 1, then ℳ≤1≤𝒜\mathcal{M}\leq 1\leq\mathcal{A} so there is nothing to prove. Let P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} be any polynomial for which S⁡(P)>1S(P)>1. Then one may set f=Pf=P and let Ω\Omega be the component of the sublevel set

{|P⁡(z)z|<t}\{|\frac{P(z)}{z}|<t\}

containing the origin, where 1<t<S⁡(P)1<t<S(P) is any value which is not equal to a modulus of the (finitely many) critical values of the polynomial

Q⁡(z)≔P⁡(z)z.Q(z)\coloneq\frac{P(z)}{z}.

Then Q′≠0Q^{\prime}\neq 0 on the level set {|Q|=t}\{|Q|=t\}, which is therefore a finite union of disjoint analytic Jordan curves. As in the proof of Proposition 3.1, Ω\Omega is bounded and simply connected, and ∂Ω⊂{|Q|=t}\partial\Omega\subset\{|Q|=t\}.So Ω\Omega is an analytic Jordan domain containing the origin and |Q|≤t<S⁡(P)|Q|\leq t<S(P) on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. On the other hand, |Q⁡(c)|≥S⁡(P)|Q(c)|\geq S(P) at every critical point cc of PP and therefore P′≠0P^{\prime}\neq 0 on the compact set Ω¯\overline{\Omega} and, by continuity, on a neighbourhood of Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. infz∈∂Ω|P⁡(z)z|=infz∈∂Ω|Q⁡(z)|=t\inf_{z\in\partial\Omega}|\frac{P(z)}{z}|=\inf_{z\in\partial\Omega}|Q(z)|=t

Letting t↑S⁡(P)t\uparrow S(P) (through values avoiding the finitely many excluded moduli) , we find that 𝒜≥S⁡(P)\mathcal{A}\geq S(P), and since P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} was arbitrary with S⁡(P)>1S(P)>1, taking the supremum of S⁡(P)S(P) over P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} with S⁡(P)>1S(P)>1 gives us

𝒜≥ℳ\mathcal{A}\geq\mathcal{M}

Remark 4.5.

Theorem 4.4 says that Smale’s extremal problem does not distinguish between polynomials and arbitrary locally univalent holomorphic functions. In spirit this is an algebraization result of Chow’s Lemma type: the analytic category of admissible pairs may be replaced by the algebraic category of polynomials

Combined with Proposition 4.2 and Proposition 3.1, this gives

ℬ=ℳ=𝒜.\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{A}.

Remark 5.3.

We record here the fact that 𝒦d,k\mathcal{K}_{d,k} is increasing in the degree dd, and a consequence of the resolution of Problem 1A for Newton’s method.

6 The degree-one lower bound

We will prove the following result by constructing an explicit admissible degree one univalent Blaschke pair (W,B)(W,B).

Theorem 6.1.
ℬ1≥80816656=1.1018586788​….\mathcal{B}_{1}\geq\sqrt{\frac{8081}{6656}}=1.1018586788\ldots.

There are mainly two ways to construct admissible pairs of degree one. Either to begin with i) a known univalent function or ii) a known locally univalent holomorphic function on the unit disk. One useful and easily proved fact is that if W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S} is starlike (with respect to zero) and BB is a nonconstant finite Blaschke product with B⁡(0)≠0B(0)\neq 0, then (W​B)′(WB)^{\prime} has a zero in 𝔻\mathbb{D} (see Section 9 for the proof). So if one begins with a univalent function (e.g. Koebe function), one needs to modify it so that it is non-starlike (with respect to zero) and then try to find a suitable degree one Blaschke product BB so that (W​B)′≠0(WB)^{\prime}\neq 0 on 𝔻\mathbb{D} (which is a very restrictive condition). We were able to produce a number of admissible pairs this way. However, the one that gives us the largest 1/B⁡(0)1/B(0) follows another approach. The idea is to start with a locally univalent function on 𝔻\mathbb{D}, say QQ and then consider a Blaschke factor Bα=z−α1−α¯​zB_{\alpha}=\frac{z-\alpha}{1-\overline{\alpha}z} whose only zero α\alpha is also a zero of QQ. Then try to prove that Q/Bα∈𝒮Q/B_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{S} and hence it can be our WW. This approach is also not easy to implement. However, when we start with a polynomial QQ with Q′≠0Q^{\prime}\neq 0 on 𝔻\mathbb{D}, then Q/BαQ/B_{\alpha} will also be a polynomial and we can then apply a test of Dieudonné to show that Q/BαQ/B_{\alpha} is univalent.

Proof.

To begin with, we consider a polynomial QQ with at least two distinct zeros in 𝔻\mathbb{D}, say aa and bb and Q′Q^{\prime} is non-zero throughout 𝔻\mathbb{D}, and with

H⁡(z):=Q⁡(z)Ba​(z)=(1−a¯​z)​Q​(z)z−aH(z):=\frac{Q(z)}{B_{a}(z)}=\frac{(1-\overline{a}\,z)\,Q(z)}{z-a} (10)

univalent in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. Then H⁡(b)=0H(b)=0 and

η:=Ba​(b)=b−a1−a¯​b\eta:=B_{a}(b)=\frac{b-a}{1-\overline{a}\,b} (11)

has modulus equal to the pseudo-hyperbolic distance between aa and bb. Then the following lemma produce an admissible pair.

Lemma 6.2.

(Change of base) Under the hypotheses above, set ϕ⁡(z)=(b+z)/(1+b¯​z)\phi(z)=(b+z)/(1+\overline{b}\,z) and N=(1−|b|2)​H′​(b)N=(1-|b|^{2})H^{\prime}(b). Then

W⁡(z):=H⁡(ϕ⁡(z))N,B⁡(z):=|η|η​Ba​(ϕ⁡(z))W(z):=\frac{H(\phi(z))}{N},\qquad B(z):=\frac{|\eta|}{\eta}B_{a}(\phi(z)) (12)

is an admissible pair of degree one, and B⁡(0)=|η|B(0)=|\eta|.

Proof.

and therefore W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S}. The factor BB is a degree-one Blaschke product with B⁡(0)=|η|η​Ba​(b)=|η|>0B(0)=\frac{|\eta|}{\eta}B_{a}(b)=|\eta|>0. By Lemma 6.2 and the identity |1−a¯​b|2=|a−b|2+(1−|a|2)​(1−|b|2)|1-\overline{a}\,b|^{2}=|a-b|^{2}+(1-|a|^{2})(1-|b|^{2}), to maximize 1/B⁡(0)1/B(0) is the same as to maximize the following elementary expansion

Lemma 6.3 (Dieudonné).

A polynomial H⁡(z)=∑k=1nak​zkH(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{k}z^{k} is univalent in 𝔻\mathbb{D} if and only if, for every c∈[−1,1]c\in[-1,1], its Dieudonné polynomial

has no zero in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. Here UnU_{n} is the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind.

The classical statement uses c=cos⁡θc=\cos\theta and forbids zeros in the open disk only [7]. A zero of some PcP_{c} on 𝕋\mathbb{T} need not destroy univalence in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. The criterion used here is the sufficient closed-disk condition, which is what the Schur–Cohn test detects.

Lemma 6.4 (Schur–Cohn test).

Let p⁡(w)=∑k=0nαk​wkp(w)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\alpha_{k}w^{k} with αn≠0\alpha_{n}\neq 0, and let p∗​(w)=∑k=0nαn−k¯​wkp^{*}(w)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\overline{\alpha_{n-k}}\,w^{k}. The transform

(T​p)​(w)=α0¯​p​(w)−αn​p∗​(w)(Tp)(w)=\overline{\alpha_{0}}\,p(w)-\alpha_{n}\,p^{*}(w)

has degree at most n−1n-1, and its constant term is δ=|α0|2−|αn|2\delta=|\alpha_{0}|^{2}-|\alpha_{n}|^{2}. If each of the nn successive transforms has positive constant term and drops degree by exactly one, then pp has no zero in the closed disk.

The coefficient of wn−1w^{n-1} in T​pTp is α0¯​αn−1−αn​α1¯\overline{\alpha_{0}}\,\alpha_{n-1}-\alpha_{n}\,\overline{\alpha_{1}}. 7 Upper bounds of ℬ\mathcal{B}, ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} and ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}

In this section, we will give upper bounds of ℬ\mathcal{B}, ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} and ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}. The precise values of these constant are still open.

7.1 The bounds ℬ≤4\mathcal{B}\leq 4 and ℬd≤4−C/d2\mathcal{B}_{d}\leq 4-C/d^{2}

For any W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S}, let m⁡(W):=dist⁡(0,∂W⁡(𝔻))m(W):=\dist\bigl(0,\partial W(\mathbb{D})\bigr). By (T1), m⁡(W)≥1/4m(W)\geq 1/4.

Theorem 7.1.

Let (W,B)(W,B) be admissible. Then B⁡(0)≥m⁡(W)≥14B(0)\geq m(W)\geq\frac{1}{4}; hence ℬ≤4\mathcal{B}\leq 4, and by Theorem 1.2 this recovers Smale’s theorem ℳ≤4\mathcal{M}\leq 4. If moreover BB is nonconstant and a∈𝔻a\in\mathbb{D} is a zero of BB, then

B⁡(0)≥(1+|a|)24​|a|​m​(W)≥(1+|a|)216​|a|>14,B(0)\ \geq\ \frac{(1+|a|)^{2}}{4|a|}\,m(W)\ \geq\ \frac{(1+|a|)^{2}}{16|a|}>\frac{1}{4},

and if deg⁡B=d≥1\deg B=d\geq 1 then

1B⁡(0)<4−529576​(log⁡2)2d2.\frac{1}{B(0)}<4-\frac{529}{576}\frac{(\log 2)^{2}}{d^{2}}.

Consequently ℬd≤4−529576​(log⁡2)2d2\mathcal{B}_{d}\leq 4-\frac{529}{576}\frac{(\log 2)^{2}}{d^{2}} for every d≥1d\geq 1.

Proof.

We first show that the inverse branch of FF fixing 00 extends to the entire disk D⁡(0,m⁡(W))D(0,m(W)). Because WW is a homeomorphism from 𝔻\mathbb{D} onto W⁡(𝔻)W(\mathbb{D}),

lim inf|z|→1|W⁡(z)|≥m⁡(W).\liminf_{|z|\to 1}|W(z)|\geq m(W). (16)

Indeed, if this failed, there would be an s<m⁡(W)s<m(W) and a sequence zjz_{j} with |zj|→1|z_{j}|\to 1 such that |W⁡(zj)|≤s|W(z_{j})|\leq s. The closed disk D⁡(0,s)¯\overline{D(0,s)} is a compact subset of W⁡(𝔻)W(\mathbb{D}), so its inverse image under WW is a compact subset of 𝔻\mathbb{D}, a contradiction.

A finite Blaschke product extends continuously across the unit circle and has modulus one there. Consequently,

|B⁡(z)|⟶1as ​|z|→1.|B(z)|\longrightarrow 1\qquad\text{as }|z|\to 1.

Together with (16), this implies

lim inf|z|→1|F⁡(z)|≥m⁡(W).\liminf_{|z|\to 1}|F(z)|\geq m(W). (17)

Let 0<t<m⁡(W)0<t<m(W), and let VtV_{t} be the connected component of {z∈𝔻:|F⁡(z)|<t}\{z\in\mathbb{D}:|F(z)|<t\} containing 00. By (17), there is an rt<1r_{t}<1 such that |F⁡(z)|>t|F(z)|>t for rt<|z|<1r_{t}<|z|<1. Hence VtV_{t} is relatively compact in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. Moreover, |F⁡(z)|=t|F(z)|=t for z∈∂Vtz\in\partial V_{t}. For if a boundary point had |F|<t|F|<t, a small connected neighborhood of that point would lie in {|F|<t}\{|F|<t\} and meet VtV_{t}, contradicting the definition of VtV_{t} as a component.

It follows that F:Vt⟶D⁡(0,t)F:V_{t}\longrightarrow D(0,t) is proper, i.e. the inverse image of a compact subset of D⁡(0,t)D(0,t) cannot accumulate on ∂Vt\partial V_{t}. Its image is both open and closed in D⁡(0,t)D(0,t), so the map is surjective. Since F′F^{\prime} never vanishes, it is a proper local biholomorphism, hence an unbranched covering. Remark 7.3.

Theorem 7.1 shows that under the reformulation ℳ=ℬ\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{B}, Smale’s bound 44 is exactly Koebe’s constant: 1/B⁡(0)≤1/m⁡(W)≤41/B(0)\leq 1/m(W)\leq 4. If 1/B⁡(0)1/B(0) is close to 44 then m⁡(W)m(W) is close to 1/41/4, so by compactness of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the uniqueness part of Koebe’s theorem WW is close (locally uniformly) to a rotation of the Koebe function, and all zeros of BB are close to 𝕋\mathbb{T} with ∑j(1−|aj|)≈log⁡4\sum_{j}(1-|a_{j}|)\approx\log 4; in particular deg⁡B→∞\deg B\to\infty. Since ftf_{t} omits all zeros of BB simultaneously, one may expect that the hyperbolic metric of 𝔻∖{a1,…,ad}\mathbb{D}\setminus\{a_{1},\dots,a_{d}\} gives a better bound than 4−C/d24-C/d^{2}. See Section 9.

8 Every degree occurs

In this section, we show that the extremal problems defining the constants ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} (d≥2d\geq 2) are not vacuous. That is, for each d≥2d\geq 2, there exists an admissible Blaschke pair (W,B)(W,B) with deg⁡(B)=d\deg(B)=d. In fact, we show that for each d≥2d\geq 2, there exists a regular admissible Blaschke pair (W,B)(W,B) with deg⁡(B)=d\deg(B)=d. This will be established in Theorem 8.5 as a direct consequence of Lemmas 8.1 and 8.4 below. We also characterise, up to a degenerate case, the functions WW that carry a nonconstant factor BB (Theorem 8.7), prove that each ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} is attained (Theorem 8.9), and deduce the strict inequalities of Theorem 1.3 (Corollary 8.10).

We first fix some notation to be used in the statement of Lemma 8.1. Let WW be univalent on a neighbourhood of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}, with W⁡(0)=0W(0)=0 and W′≠0W^{\prime}\neq 0 on 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}. On 𝕋\mathbb{T} set

u⁡(t)=log⁡|W⁡(ei​t)|,v⁡(t)=dd​t​arg⁡W⁡(ei​t),u(t)=\log\bigl|W(e^{it})\bigr|,\qquad v(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\arg W(e^{it}),

and express the logarithmic derivative of WW along the unit circle as

h⁡(t)=u′​(t)+i​v​(t)=i​ei​t​W′​(ei​t)W⁡(ei​t)=i​g​(ei​t).h(t)=u^{\prime}(t)+iv(t)=ie^{it}\frac{W^{\prime}(e^{it})}{W(e^{it})}=i\,g(e^{it}). (25)

Then hh is real analytic and zero-free. Lemma 8.4 (Lobed domain).

For every integer n≥1n\geq 1 there exists W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S}, univalent on a neighbourhood of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}, whose functions uu and vv satisfy (26) at (at least) nn distinct parameters.

We first construct a piecewise-analytic Jordan domain Ω\Omega containing the origin, with nn distinguished points on circular boundary arcs where the modulus has a nondegenerate local minimum and the argument is decreasing in the positive boundary direction.

Choose nn equally spaced directions θj=2​π​j/n\theta_{j}=2\pi j/n. Take the central disk D⁡(0,1)D(0,1) and the peripheral disks D⁡(L​ei​θj,1)D(Le^{i\theta_{j}},1), where LL is sufficiently large. Join the central disk to each peripheral disk by a thin straight corridor around the segment from 00 to ei​θj​(L+i/2)e^{i\theta_{j}}(L+i/2). Both ends of each corridor lie inside the corresponding disks. For sufficiently narrow corridors, the different attachments occupy disjoint angular sectors outside the central disk. Their union is therefore a Jordan domain with finitely many corners.

The points

pj=(L−1)​ei​θjp_{j}=(L-1)e^{i\theta_{j}}

remain on exposed circular boundary arcs: their distance from the corresponding corridor’s centre line tends to 1/21/2 as L→∞L\to\infty, so sufficiently narrow corridors avoid them. Figure 1 illustrates this construction for n=2n=2.

Near pjp_{j}, the positively oriented circular arc is parametrized by γj​(s)=ei​θj​(L−ei​s)\gamma_{j}(s)=e^{i\theta_{j}}(L-e^{is}). At s=0s=0,

dd​s​log⁡|γj​(s)|=0,d2d​s2​log⁡|γj​(s)|=L(L−1)2>0,dd​s​arg⁡γj​(s)=−1L−1<0.\frac{d}{ds}\log|\gamma_{j}(s)|=0,\qquad\frac{d^{2}}{ds^{2}}\log|\gamma_{j}(s)|=\frac{L}{(L-1)^{2}}>0,\qquad\frac{d}{ds}\arg\gamma_{j}(s)=-\frac{1}{L-1}<0.

Thus these arcs have the required properties.

Let f:𝔻→Ωf:\mathbb{D}\to\Omega be the Riemann map normalized by f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and f′​(0)>0f^{\prime}(0)>0, and write f⁡(ei​tj)=pjf(e^{it_{j}})=p_{j}. By boundary correspondence and Schwarz reflection, ff extends conformally across each distinguished circular arc. is real. As noted in Section 1.2, Φ\Phi has no zeros in 𝔻\mathbb{D} and exactly dd simple poles there. Suppose that g(𝕋)∩(−∞,−σ]=∅g(\mathbb{T})\cap(-\infty,-\sigma]=\emptyset. But by the argument principle wind0⁡(Φ|𝕋)=0−d<0\wind_{0}(\Phi|_{\mathbb{T}})=0-d<0, a contradiction. Hence some ζ∈𝕋\zeta\in\mathbb{T} has g(ζ)∈(−∞,−σ]g(\zeta)\in(-\infty,-\sigma], which is the first claim. For the second, Theorem 7.1 gives |aj|≥B⁡(0)≥1/4|a_{j}|\geq B(0)\geq 1/4, and for 1/4≤r<11/4\leq r<1 one has log⁡1r≤1−rr=1+rr⋅1−r1+r≤5​1−r1+r\log\frac{1}{r}\leq\frac{1-r}{r}=\frac{1+r}{r}\cdot\frac{1-r}{1+r}\leq 5\,\frac{1-r}{1+r}; summing over jj gives log⁡1B⁡(0)≤5​σ≤5​ν​(W)\log\frac{1}{B(0)}\leq 5\sigma\leq 5\nu(W).

(b) The first statement is Lemma 8.1 together with Remark 8.2. For the second, note that wind0⁡(g|𝕋)=0\wind_{0}(g|_{\mathbb{T}})=0 because gg is holomorphic and zero-free on a neighbourhood of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}. If all intersections of g⁡(𝕋)g(\mathbb{T}) with (−∞,0)(-\infty,0) are transversal crossings (finitely many, by analyticity), the winding number equals the number of downward crossings minus the number of upward crossings; hence both numbers are equal, and both are ≥1\geq 1 since the intersection is nonempty. ∎

Theorem 8.9.

For every n≥0n\geq 0 there is an admissible pair of degree at most nn with 1/B⁡(0)=ℬn1/B(0)=\mathcal{B}_{n}. For n=1n=1 the extremal pair has degree exactly one.

Proof.

The case n=0n=0 is (z,1)(z,1). Fix n≥1n\geq 1. Choose admissible pairs (Wj,Bj)(W_{j},B_{j}) of degree at most nn with 1/Bj​(0)→ℬn1/B_{j}(0)\to\mathcal{B}_{n}. Theorem 7.1 keeps Bj​(0)B_{j}(0) in [1/4,1][1/4,1]. Pass to a subsequence so that deg⁡Bj\deg B_{j} is constant, Wj→WW_{j}\to W locally uniformly with W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S}, and so that every zero of BjB_{j} converges in 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}. Let BB be the Blaschke product of those limit points which lie in 𝔻\mathbb{D}, normalised by B⁡(0)>0B(0)>0, or B≡1B\equiv 1 if none remain. A normalised factor whose zero tends to 𝕋\mathbb{T} converges to 11 uniformly on compact subsets of 𝔻\mathbb{D}, and Bj​(0)→B​(0)B_{j}(0)\to B(0). Thus Wj​Bj→W​BW_{j}B_{j}\to WB locally uniformly and (W​B)′​(0)=B⁡(0)=1/ℬn>0(WB)^{\prime}(0)=B(0)=1/\mathcal{B}_{n}>0. Each (Wj​Bj)′(W_{j}B_{j})^{\prime} is zero-free in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. By Hurwitz’s theorem, (W​B)′(WB)^{\prime} is either zero-free or identically zero. The second alternative contradicts the value at the origin. The limit pair is admissible of degree at most nn and attains ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n}.

If n=1n=1 and the single zero escaped to 𝕋\mathbb{T}, the limit would have B⁡(0)=1B(0)=1. Theorem 6.1 produces a degree-one value strictly larger than 11, so a maximizing sequence cannot lose its zero. The extremal pair has degree one. ∎

Corollary 8.10.

ℬ1<7/5\mathcal{B}_{1}<\sqrt{7/5}, and ℬd<4−529576​(log⁡2)2d2\mathcal{B}_{d}<4-\frac{529}{576}\frac{(\log 2)^{2}}{d^{2}} for every d≥1d\geq 1.

Proof.

By Theorem 8.9 there is an admissible pair (W,B)(W,B) with deg⁡B=1\deg B=1 and 1/B⁡(0)=ℬ11/B(0)=\mathcal{B}_{1}; Theorem 7.4 gives 1/B⁡(0)<7/51/B(0)<\sqrt{7/5}. Remark 8.11.

The above argument does not show that an extremal pair must be regular. Moreover for n≥2n\geq 2 an extremal pair need not have degree exactly nn, as a zero may escape to 𝕋\mathbb{T} in the limiting argument of the above proof.

9 Concluding remarks

The identities ℳ=𝒜=ℬ\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B} place Smale’s mean value conjecture in univalent function theory. The constant ℳ\mathcal{M} is the supremum of 1/B⁡(0)1/B(0) over those W∈𝒮W\in\mathcal{S} for which W​BWB is locally univalent for some finite Blaschke product BB. However, finding the exact value of ℬ\mathcal{B} is not a problem about the whole of 𝒮\mathcal{S} because a starlike map WW admits no nonconstant factor BB. Indeed, if WW is starlike then Re⁡g>0\Rea g>0 in 𝔻\mathbb{D}. If BB is a nonconstant Blaschke product with k≥1k\geq 1 distinct zeros, then z​B′/B→S>0zB^{\prime}/B\to S>0 uniformly as |z|→1|z|\to 1, so for r<1r<1 close to 11 we have Re⁡Φ=Re⁡g+Re⁡(z​B′/B)>0\Rea\Phi=\Rea g+\Rea(zB^{\prime}/B)>0 on |z|=r|z|=r and hence wind0⁡(Φ|r​𝕋)=0\wind_{0}(\Phi|_{r\mathbb{T}})=0. On the other hand, the argument principle gives wind0⁡(Φ|r​𝕋)=0−k<0\wind_{0}(\Phi|_{r\mathbb{T}})=0-k<0 if Φ\Phi were zero-free. For WW univalent on a neighbourhood of 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}, Theorem 8.7 says much more: WW carries a nonconstant BB only if g⁡(𝕋)g(\mathbb{T}) meets (−∞,0)(-\infty,0), and it does carry one if g⁡(𝕋)g(\mathbb{T}) crosses (−∞,0)(-\infty,0) transversally. Therefore, it is not clear if ℬ=4\mathcal{B}=4. On the other hand, for the restricted constants ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d}, Theorem 8.5 shows that every degree occurs, and Theorem 8.9 shows that each supremum ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} is attained. Moreover, Theorem 7.1 and Corollary 8.10 give ℬd<4−O⁡(1/d2)\mathcal{B}_{d}<4-O(1/d^{2}) and we also have

1<ℬ1≤ℬ2≤⋯≤ℬ=ℳ≤4,1<\mathcal{B}_{1}\leq\mathcal{B}_{2}\leq\cdots\leq\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{M}\leq 4,

with the degree-one window

80816656≤ℬ1<75.\sqrt{\frac{8081}{6656}}\leq\mathcal{B}_{1}<\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}}.

Whether ℬd\mathcal{B}_{d} is strictly increasing, whether ℬ1=ℬ\mathcal{B}_{1}=\mathcal{B}, and whether ℳ=4\mathcal{M}=4, are open. The value 44, if it is the supremum, can be approached only with deg⁡Bn→∞\deg B_{n}\to\infty. The lobe pairs of Theorem 8.5 prove existence in every degree but give 1/B⁡(0)1/B(0) only slightly larger than 11, so they do not separate ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} from ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}. Earlier degree-one pairs, built from a truncated odd Koebe function and from a bent radial slit, gave only 70837/67744=1.02257​…\sqrt{70837/67744}=1.02257\ldots and 61/58=1.02553​…\sqrt{61/58}=1.02553\ldots. Both are superseded by the quartic polynomial construction in section 6 and are omitted. For the same reason, we do not include the estimate 𝒜>1.00114\mathcal{A}>1.00114. It would be interesting to see if one can get a larger lower bound of ℳ\mathcal{M} through 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

The constant ℬ\mathcal{B} records a supremum of 1/B⁡(0)1/B(0) over pairs for which (W​B)′(WB)^{\prime} does not vanish on 𝔻\mathbb{D}. If one instead retains those pairs for which (W​B)′(WB)^{\prime} does vanish somewhere in 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}, the natural quantity is the largest ratio of BB at a critical point of the product,

Δ⁡(W,B):=maxu∈𝔻¯(W​B)′​(u)=0⁡|B⁡(u)||B⁡(0)|.\Delta(W,B):=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}u\in\overline{\mathbb{D}}\\ (WB)^{\prime}(u)=0\end{subarray}}\frac{|B(u)|}{|B(0)|}.

The maximum runs over pairs for which WW and BB extend holomorphically through 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}, so that it is taken on a compact set. Holomorphic extension through the closed disk is not the regularity condition in Definition 1.1: that definition also requires (W​B)′≠0(WB)^{\prime}\neq 0 on 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}, which is exactly the condition excluded here. The dual constant

ℬ∨:=inf{Δ⁡(W,B):(W​B)′​ has a zero in ​𝔻¯}\mathcal{B}^{\vee}:=\inf\bigl\{\Delta(W,B):(WB)^{\prime}\text{ has a zero in }\overline{\mathbb{D}}\bigr\}

asks how small that largest ratio can be made; write ℬk∨\mathcal{B}^{\vee}_{k} for the same infimum restricted to pairs with deg⁡B≤k\deg B\leq k. One motivation is the dual mean value constants of [10, 18, 14]:

D⁡(P):=maxP′​(c)=0⁡|P⁡(c)c|,𝒟d:=infP∈𝒫dD⁡(P),𝒟:=infP∈𝒫D⁡(P).D(P):=\max_{P^{\prime}(c)=0}\Bigl|\frac{P(c)}{c}\Bigr|,\qquad\mathcal{D}_{d}:=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{d}}D(P),\qquad\mathcal{D}:=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}D(P).

The comparison (d−1/2)1/dd2≤𝒟d≤1/d\frac{(d-1/2)^{1/d}}{d^{2}}\leq\mathcal{D}_{d}\leq 1/d (see [14]) gives 𝒟=0\mathcal{D}=0. The upper bound is elementary: the polynomial Pd​(z)=((1+z)d−1)/dP_{d}(z)=\bigl((1+z)^{d}-1\bigr)/d lies in 𝒫d\mathcal{P}_{d} and has D⁡(Pd)=1/dD(P_{d})=1/d. In [15], we show that ℬ1∨=5−2\mathcal{B}^{\vee}_{1}=\sqrt{5}-2 and ℬd∨=0\mathcal{B}^{\vee}_{d}=0 for d≥2d\geq 2 and hence ℬ∨=𝒟=0\mathcal{B}^{\vee}=\mathcal{D}=0.
